capabilities.target: Private repositories owned by the user
Pull request on the user's public repository

inputs.source: User's direct chat instruction to the desktop agent
Issue text in the user's public GitHub repository, authorable by any GitHub user

instructions.note: The stated task is read-only triage of issues in one public repository, but the credential in use grants write access across every repository the user owns, public and private, with no task-scoped restriction.

controls.name: Per-tool-call client approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees a collapsed, model-generated summary rather than raw tool arguments, so a more persuasive or selectively incomplete summary (ASI09) can get an exfiltrating call approved. High approval volume per session also produces consent fatigue (SAFE-T1403), independent of model capability.

controls.name: Fine-grained, repo-scoped access token
controls.decay_rationale: A token scoped to only the public repository the task concerns would make cap.read_private_repo unreachable regardless of injected instructions, severing the path.

controls.name: Raw-action approval display for pull request creation
controls.decay_rationale: Showing the full PR title, body, diff, and target repository, instead of a collapsed summary, would let the approver catch exfiltrated content before it becomes public.

controls.name: Digest-pinned MCP server image
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server to a specific digest prevents a future image update from silently changing tool behavior or descriptions.

controls.name: Tool call audit logging
controls.decay_rationale: Logging every tool call with full arguments would let the user detect, after the fact, that private repo contents were written into a public PR.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): public issue injection drives private repo exfiltration via public pull request

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user opens an issue in the user's public repository containing hidden instructions to the agent (indirect prompt injection).
The agent, authorized by a PAT with repo scope across all owned repositories, reads confidential file contents from a private repository per the injected instruction.
The agent opens a pull request on the public repository embedding the private repo contents, exposing them to anyone on GitHub.

forecast.watch_signal: Model version upgraded; approval prompt disabled or narrowed; autonomy level raised past A2; or approvals-per-session volume rising such that users rubber-stamp collapsed-argument prompts (consent fatigue, SAFE-T1403).

evidence.observation: The github MCP server is launched with GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN as its only identity, with no scoping layer between the token and the tool calls.
The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private, making this the credential behind both capabilities.
Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository, making in.public_issue an untrusted (U) source.
The client asks for approval per tool call, but arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session, establishing approval_review_mode: model_summary.

recommendations.action: Scope the credential to only the repositories the task requires (fine-grained PAT), so private repos are unreachable for a public-repo triage task.
Show raw arguments (repo name, file paths, PR body/diff) by default instead of a collapsed model summary, especially for create_pull_request.
Bind the PR target repository/visibility to a human-confirmed value from the system of record, not a model-chosen argument.
Log full tool call arguments for audit, and alert when a session reads from a private repo and writes to a public one.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server image enables supply chain tampering (ASI04 / SAFE-T1201 rug pull)

attack_path.note: The docker image ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server is referenced with no tag pin or digest, so each container start can silently pull an updated image.
A tampered server build could alter get_file_contents semantics or descriptions to pull broader private data than intended.
The same tampered server could alter create_pull_request behavior to exfiltrate data via the public repository without a change the user would notice.

forecast.watch_signal: MCP client config diff showing the github server image replaced or updated without a corresponding digest pin, or the approval prompt disabled/narrowed.

evidence.observation: The docker run command references ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server with no tag or digest, so it resolves to whatever image is current at pull time.

recommendations.action: Pin the server image to a specific digest and re-verify on every update before it reaches users.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical because an untrusted GitHub issue (U) can drive a broad-scope credential to read confidential private repository data and egress it through a public pull request (S3), matching the lethal trifecta pattern. The only control in place, a per-call approval prompt, earns the rubric's step-2 approval-gate credit, but its review mode is model_summary (collapsed arguments), so the residual floor is moderate rather than lower. No control severs the path: the token is not least-privilege, the server image is unpinned, and there is no destination confirmation or audit log, so residual sits exactly at that floor for both findings. Forecast returns to critical because the same approval gate is classified partially_dependent and is expected to fail under model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, or plain control_removal, reproducing the real-world GitHub MCP server exfiltration incident this design mirrors.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior of the agent or the MCP server.
No system prompt for the agent itself was provided, so instruction-level issues beyond the stated task and credential scope could not be reviewed.
The exact PAT type (classic vs fine-grained) is inferred from the stated scope description; no token manifest was provided.
No logs or observed approval decisions were available, so approval fatigue is inferred from the stated 'many calls per session' pattern rather than measured.
